claims.quote: 11:18 a.m. — I held the camera over the face until the glass reflected too much light and, on the third take, caught the hands squared at four twenty-two.
11:34 a.m. — I laid the locket beside the diary page I had photographed in the attic and took close-ups of the scratched letters on the silver. The initials were shallow and crude: E.L.

11:27 a.m. — in my bedroom I set the cracked mirror on the bed and propped the sepia photograph against the glass. Under raking light the back was legible in a way it had not been when I first found it: faint, smeared ink resolved into a date. I read it aloud and wrote it down. "Oct 12 1913," I said

I sat on the attic joist and read the torn fragment aloud, just as I had the photograph. The words were small and sudden on the page: "Oct 12 — tea and the clock. The clock stopped at four and twenty-two when Mam went for sugar. —spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell."
claims.value: "Oct 12 — tea and the clock. The clock stopped at four and twenty-two when Mam went for sugar. —spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell."

claims.quote: 11:44 a.m. — The dark patch under the subfloor had the same stubborn, dry look as before; in the light it read as the colour of old tea, a bruised brown with speckled edges.

12:17 p.m. — I wrote the new facts into my notebook the way you repair a leak by marking it. The locket's initials read E.L.; the sepia's back read "Oct 12 1913"; the torn diary page said, verbatim, "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell."
claims.value: records timestamps and findings in notebook

claims.quote: "Children left long ago," she said, clipped. She moved a jar of preserves between us as if it were a screen. "This house has its ways. We don't keep much past what's necessary."
